title: At the clothes shop
goal: Say what you like and don't like, name colors and clothes, then try things on and buy them.
bekal: saying what you like and don't like
using colors in the matching form
asking prices and trying things on

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En una tienda de ropa
dialogs.intro: A clothes shop. Watch the verb *gustar*, which works backwards compared with English "like".

lines.speaker: Dependiente:
lines.id: Good afternoon, can I help you?
lines.literal: good afternoons, in what I-can help-you(formal)?

notes: **Gustar works backwards, and this is the hardest part of the unit.** *Me gusta el café* isn't "I like coffee" but literally **"coffee pleases me"**. So the subject of the sentence is **the thing**, not you. Once you accept that, the rest falls into place.

**Since the thing is the subject, the verb agrees with it.** One thing: *me gusta el libro*. Several: *me gustan los libros*. Followed by a verb, it's always singular: *me gusta leer* (I like reading), even with two verbs: *me gusta leer y escribir*.

**What changes is the person who feels it:** *me* (me), *te* (you), *le* (him/her/you formal), *nos* (us), *os* (you all), *les* (them). For emphasis, add a phrase in front: *A mí me gusta, pero a él no le gusta*.

**Colors agree with the noun.** Those ending in -o change fully: *blanco / blanca / blancos / blancas*. Those ending in -e or a consonant only change in the plural: *verde → verdes*, *azul → azules*. And colors go **after** the noun: *una camisa blanca*, not *una blanca camisa*.
**La azul, la mediana, la mía** — you can drop the noun completely as long as the article stays. *Prefiero la azul* = "I prefer the blue one", with *camisa* understood from the previous sentence.

**Quedar for how clothes fit.** *Me queda grande* (it's too big on me), *me queda bien* (it fits), *te queda muy bien* (it looks great on you). The pattern is exactly like *gustar*: the item of clothing is the subject.

**Verbs that split in the middle.** *Poder* → *puedo*, *querer* → *quiero*, *preferir* → *prefiero*, *costar* → *cuesta*. The change only happens in the stressed syllable — which is why the *nosotros* form escapes: *podemos*, *queremos*, *preferimos*.
**Me la llevo** uses two little words at once (*me* + *la*) — grammar that's really beyond A1. Learn it as a set phrase: "I'll take it". For a masculine item: *me lo llevo*.

grammars.title: The gustar pattern
body: The order is fixed: **to whom** + *gusta / gustan* + **what is liked**. To negate, just put *no* at the very front: *No me gusta el pescado*.
after: How much you like something, from hate to love: *odio* (I hate) · *no me gusta nada* · *no me gusta* · *me gusta* · *me gusta mucho* · *me encanta* (I love it). Note that *me encanta* already means "I really like it", so *me encanta mucho* is overkill.

Other verbs with exactly the same pattern: *me duele* (it hurts me), *me interesa* (it interests me), *me parece* (it seems to me), *me apetece* (I feel like it). Once the *gustar* pattern sticks, you get these for free.

blocks.text: Two colors that started life as nouns — *rosa* (rose) and *naranja* (orange) — never change form: *unos zapatos rosa*, not *rosas*. And adding *claro* or *oscuro* freezes the color too: *unas camisas azul claro*.

blocks.title: Must-know shop phrases
items: *¿Qué talla usa?* — what size are you? The answer: *la pequeña* (S), *la mediana* (M), *la grande* (L). For shoes: *¿Qué número calza?*
*¿Puedo probármelo?* — can I try it on? · *el probador* — fitting room · *¿Tiene otro color?* — do you have another color?
*Me queda grande / pequeño / bien* — too big / too small / fits. · *Me lo llevo* — I'll take it.
*¿Se puede cambiar?* — can it be exchanged? · *el recibo* — receipt · *las rebajas* — the sales.
